inserts.title: Corridor width measures how consistent a route is
paragraphs: A **corridor** is the band of ground that a bird covers repeatedly when it flies home along the same learned path. Its width describes how tightly a bird's training tracks cluster around one route. A narrow corridor means the bird returns to nearly the same ground on each journey, while a wide corridor means its paths vary more from flight to flight.

Biro and colleagues measured corridor widths from each bird's final training tracks and expressed them relative to route length. The average width was 151 m at Weston Wood and 176 m at High Cogges. Scaling by route length places routes of different lengths on one scale, so the widths can be compared directly.

A consistent route can still be indirect, so the width measures repeatability of the path rather than accuracy of arrival at the loft. The GPS records supply the positions used to calculate each width.
notes: Corridor width is a property of the flight tracks themselves.

inserts.title: Convergence reveals a pull toward a learned corridor
paragraphs: **Convergence** is the movement of a displaced bird back toward a route it has flown before. In an off-route release, the bird begins far from its usual corridor, so any turn toward the old track shows what draws it. Biro and colleagues recorded the complete homing track of each pigeon to see whether it headed straight for the loft or first rejoined the familiar route.

Many off-route tracks merged with the previously used corridor before continuing toward home. The published maps show training and test tracks at a scale of about 2 km, so each displacement can be read against the surrounding terrain. The merge happened far from the release point, which places the pull of the route over a broad area.

The merging points to attraction toward familiar visual landmarks, with the bird reaching recognized features before it turns toward the loft. Other navigational systems remained available during the same flights.

inserts.title: Time-compensated sun compass uses the sun and clock
paragraphs: A **time-compensated sun compass** combines the sun's position with the bird's internal sense of time to estimate a direction. The sun moves across the sky at a steady rate, so the same solar position corresponds to a different compass direction at a different hour. Keeping the internal clock matched to local time keeps the sun compass accurate.

Biro and colleagues shifted the birds' clock by delaying artificial sunrise and sunset by 4 h for 5–7 days. The shift predicted a solar-compass error of about 90° on the release dates. Tracks after treatment were set against each bird's earlier flights, so every pigeon's own route served as its baseline.

A bird that follows its familiar route ignores part of the compass error, whereas a bird that trusts the compass moves away from the route. Each track shows which of these two cues the bird weights more heavily.
notes: The sun compass depends on time as well as on the sun.

The sun's position changes steadily through the day.
A bird must know the time to read the sun correctly.

inserts.title: Parallel offsets keep shape while shifting position
paragraphs: A **parallel offset** is a flight that keeps the shape of an earlier route while sitting consistently to one side of it. The bird maintains the sequence of turns and the overall form of the route, and only its position changes sideways.

After the clock shift, some highly familiar pigeons flew parallel to their former tracks on the anticlockwise side. Route-relative vectors measured the lateral offset in metres, with reference rings at 100, 300 and 500 m. The offsets were consistent across the birds that showed them.
A parallel offset combines recognition of the route with a directional correction from the compass. The shape of the familiar route is kept while the whole route is moved to one side.
notes: A parallel offset separates the shape of a route from its position.

inserts.title: Olfactory map versus activation hypothesis
paragraphs: An **olfactory map** uses learned odor information to estimate position relative to home, so the smell of a place carries location. An **olfactory activation hypothesis** proposes that the experience of unfamiliar odors helps navigation even when the odors carry no location information. The two accounts predict different results when the odor history is changed.

Gagliardo and colleagues transported pigeons in containers supplied with natural air, charcoal-filtered air or filtered air with artificial plant odors. Artificial odor puffs were supplied about every 20 min during transport and while the birds waited at the release site. Each group carried a different odor history into the release.

The activation account predicts that artificial odors should help as much as natural air. The map account predicts that only natural air helps, because only natural air carries the geographical odor signature. The later tracks decide between these predictions.

inserts.title: Nasal anesthesia applies the same block to all groups
paragraphs: A **nasal block** removes the sense of smell for a short time by anesthetizing the olfactory mucosa. Gagliardo and colleagues applied Xylocaine immediately before release, so every pigeon lost new odor input during early flight. The earlier odor histories of the groups stay in place.

The birds had already been exposed to natural air, filtered air or artificial odors during transport and before takeoff. Releases occurred at sites 53 km and 61 km from home. The nasal block therefore limited new odor sampling for every group, while the earlier exposure differences remained.
The anesthetic wears off during the flight, so the later part of each track reflects the return of smell. The timing of that recovery is part of each measured flight.

inserts.title: Bearings and tracks describe different flight phases
paragraphs: A **vanishing bearing** is the compass direction in which a released bird disappears from view. It records the first moments of the flight. A complete GPS track instead records the whole journey, including circling, stops, course correction and progress toward home.

Bearings from the early part of each track did not reflect all the differences that appeared over the first hour. At the 53 km release, artificial-odor birds could leave in a set direction and then make little homeward progress. The full track revealed a deficit that the departure alone did not show.
A bird can leave in a reasonable direction and then correct later, or leave poorly and recover. The full track is what shows how well the bird navigated.

inserts.title: c-Fos maps regional activity, not single neurons
paragraphs: The **dorsolateral hippocampal area** is one subdivision of the pigeon hippocampal formation, distinct from its dorsomedial and triangular subdivisions. Jorge and colleagues measured c-Fos labeling separately in each region, so the forebrain response is not treated as uniform across the hippocampus.

Natural odors during displacement and unfamiliar artificial odors increased dorsolateral activation relative to filtered air. Artificial odor exposure at the home loft produced activation comparable to the displacement groups. The dorsolateral subdivision responded most strongly to the odor treatments.
The same region responds to odor even when the bird has not been moved. Odor exposure alone is therefore enough to activate this part of the hippocampus.

inserts.title: Magnetic stimulation labels trigeminal nuclei
paragraphs: The **trigeminal nerve** carries sensory information from the head, and its ophthalmic branch, V1, projects to brainstem trigeminal nuclei. Lefeldt and colleagues used ZENK labeling to ask whether changing magnetic fields activated these nuclei in pigeons.

Pigeons were exposed for 3 h to a constantly changing magnetic field, to a compensated zero field, or to the changing field after bilateral V1 section. ZENK was detected in the principal and spinal trigeminal nuclei after each exposure, and the pattern across the three groups shows where the changing field had its effect.

Labeling rose when the field changed and V1 was intact, and it fell when the field was removed or the nerve was cut. The response therefore runs through the peripheral sensory pathway that passes through V1.

inserts.title: Tracing shows a route from V1 to labeled nuclei
paragraphs: **Neuronal tracing** follows the anatomical pathways that leave an injection site. Lefeldt and colleagues injected cholera toxin B into V1 to label its central projections. The labeled fibers were then compared with the regions that showed ZENK after magnetic stimulation.

V1 fibers terminated in the principal and spinal trigeminal nuclei, the same nuclei that contained ZENK-positive cells. The overlays keep the position of each traced fiber relative to the activated cells, with scales of 100 µm and 200 µm. Acetylcholinesterase staining marked the nuclear boundaries, so each subdivision could be located precisely.
The overlap places the magnetic response along a known route from the nerve to the brainstem. Acetylcholinesterase keeps the labeled tissue tied to the known anatomy of each nucleus.

inserts.title: Stains locate iron, not the cell that holds it
paragraphs: **Prussian blue** is a stain that reveals ferric iron in tissue. A stained spot shows where iron accumulates, but identifying the cell that holds it needs a second line of evidence, because iron also appears in metabolic storage and immune cells.

Treiber and colleagues stained pigeon upper beaks with Prussian blue and mapped the labeled cells through serial sections. The stained cells lay in the respiratory epithelium, the subepidermal tissue and the feather follicles. The position of each labeled cell is recorded together with its tissue.
The stained positions give a map of where iron occurs, which is the first step toward identifying a magnetic receptor. Additional markers and ultrastructure then identify the stained cells.

inserts.title: Immune markers test cell identity in beak tissue
paragraphs: **Macrophages** are immune cells that engulf material and take part in tissue defense. **MHC II** is a cell-surface marker of antigen presentation that several immune cell types express. Treiber and colleagues combined this marker with iron staining to identify the beak cells.

MHC II labeling colocalized with the iron-positive cells in the respiratory epithelium, the subepidermal tissue and the feather follicles. Together with the ultrastructure and the absence of convincing neuronal-marker labeling, this result identifies the cells as macrophages. The micrographs carry a 10 µm scale bar.
Macrophages carry iron as a storage product, so the iron in these cells is stored rather than sensed. The identity of the cells rests on several markers taken together across the tissues.

inserts.title: Local field potentials sum population activity
paragraphs: A **local field potential**, or LFP, is an extracellular voltage that reflects coordinated activity in a population of neurons around the electrode. It differs from the spike of one identified neuron, because it sums the currents of many cells at once.

Yang and colleagues recorded hippocampal LFPs and the bird's position at the same time during outdoor homing flights. The electrodes sampled the left hippocampal formation, and the release sites lay more than 0.8 km from the loft. Trials were run in clear weather with low wind.
Recording the population signal during flight links a neural state to a particular stage of the trip. The shared time base lets each stage be matched to a moment in the recording.
notes: The LFP is a population signal recorded during flight.

inserts.title: Band power changes between navigation stages
paragraphs: **Spectral power** measures how much of a recorded voltage falls within a chosen frequency range. Yang and colleagues assigned theta to 4–12 Hz, beta to 12–30 Hz, low gamma to 30–60 Hz and high gamma to 60–120 Hz, so each band has a fixed range.

Theta and beta power ratios were higher in the initial decision-making stage than during en route flight. The high-gamma ratio rose en route, while low gamma showed no consistent difference between the stages. The comparisons used paired stages from the same homing flights.
The stages therefore differ in how power is distributed across the bands rather than in a single overall increase. Each band reflects its own pattern of population activity.

2: **Homing** is navigation back to a familiar home after displacement. In pigeons, a **map** estimates position relative to home, whereas a **compass** supplies a directional reference. Biro and colleagues recorded homing pigeons with a global positioning system, or GPS, logging position every second. Releases from trained sites and off-route tests showed how each bird reached home from unfamiliar ground.

Off-route releases separated birds that followed a familiar corridor from birds that flew straight toward the loft. Their complete tracks show which landmarks and directions guided each journey. The same GPS record also reveals the detours that a bird took on the way to home.

A bird can therefore use a learned route and a directional reference at the same time. A route can be followed through a series of changing headings, because each position on the track is recorded in sequence.
3: **Route fidelity** is the repeated use of a similar path by the same animal. It differs from accuracy of arrival, because a pigeon can reach home along a reliable but indirect corridor. Biro and colleagues compared the last three training flights from each release site to measure how consistent each route was.

After repeated homing experience, mean corridor widths were 151 m at Weston Wood and 176 m at High Cogges. These widths describe the area enclosed by each bird's final training tracks, scaled to its route length. Routes of different lengths can therefore be compared on one scale.

A narrow corridor reflects a route that each bird flies again and again. Birds with narrow corridors return to nearly the same ground on each flight, and the corridor width summarizes that repetition in a single number.
4: **Route efficiency** compares the direct home distance with the distance actually flown. A lower value means a longer journey, even when the bird ultimately reaches the loft. Efficiency and fidelity measure different properties of successful homing.

Biro and colleagues found that final training routes remained indirect after 20 successive releases. Birds flew approximately 18–25% farther than the direct home distance while still reproducing their individually distinctive paths. The 2 km map scale shows how far each detour extends from the straight line to home.

The detours are a stable part of each bird's route rather than a sign of poor navigation. A pigeon keeps the same indirect path across days, so its route becomes a personal habit that it follows reliably.
5: A **displacement** moves a bird away from its trained release point. Biro and colleagues released trained pigeons at positions outside their preferred corridors and recorded the complete homing track from each release. The tracks show whether a bird heads toward home directly or first returns to a familiar route.

The off-route tracks often converged on the previously used route before continuing toward the loft. The original maps preserve both the training tracks and the later test tracks at a 2 km scale. The merge point sits well away from the release site, which places the pull of the route over a broad area.
Birds rejoin a familiar route when they encounter its landmarks, even when a shorter path to home exists. The merging pattern shows which feature a bird uses first when it is displaced.
6: **Visual pilotage** is the use of recognized landscape features to guide movement along a familiar route. A landmark gives local guidance without placing the bird in a universal coordinate system, so the route can be learned as a succession of familiar places. Biro and colleagues compared repeated training flights with off-route releases in the same landscape.

Birds were attracted toward their preferred corridors even when this required an indirect journey. The 2 km map scale sets the size of each displacement against the surrounding terrain. The corridor attracts the birds across this terrain, so their tracks bend back toward it.
Visual pilotage supplies a continuous guide that works without a map of the whole region. A bird that recognizes the next landmark on its route can keep moving toward the loft from that point.
7: A **shared landscape** constrains flight, and individual birds still follow different routes through it. Biro and colleagues compared several pigeons returning to the same loft from the same release sites. The training and off-route maps contain clearly different paths for each bird.

Within-bird training corridors averaged 151 m at Weston Wood, while routes from different birds overlapped less closely. Each bird's track therefore carries its own history of flights through the area. The individual corridor is built from that bird's experience with particular features.

Two pigeons starting from the same place can follow different corridors and still reach the same loft. Individual experience sets the route, while the terrain sets the broad limits within which the route falls.
8: A **time-compensated sun compass** uses the sun's position together with an internal sense of time to estimate direction. Because the sun's position changes across the day, altering a bird's internal clock changes the direction it infers, while the landscape stays the same. Biro and colleagues delayed artificial sunrise and sunset by 4 h for 5–7 days.

This treatment predicted a solar-compass error of about 90° at the release dates. Each pigeon's GPS tracks after treatment were set against its own earlier flights, so each bird's route is its own baseline. The shift set the sun's direction against the familiar landscape.

A bird that trusts its clock-shifted compass heads away from its route, while a bird that follows its landmarks keeps near the route. Each track shows which of these two cues the bird weights more heavily.
9: **Cue weighting** describes how strongly each information source influences behavior. The weighting can run without a conscious decision or a single neuron that sets the numbers. Familiarity can alter how strongly a recognized route constrains compass-guided movement. Biro and colleagues compared highly familiar birds with less familiar birds at four sites 5.1–10.6 km from the loft.

After the same clock shift, highly familiar birds generally stayed closer to their previous tracks than less familiar birds did. The gap between the two groups is largest at the sites farthest from the loft. The familiar route therefore holds birds closer to their original paths when the compass signal changes.
Route memory can outweigh a conflicting compass signal once the route is well learned. Experience with the landscape makes the learned route a stronger guide for the same bird.
10: A **nearest-neighbour vector** connects a recorded point on one flight to the closest point on a comparison flight. Its length measures the spatial separation between the two flights. Its angle relative to the current flight direction tells a lateral displacement apart from a separation ahead of or behind the bird.

Biro and colleagues calculated these vectors for clock-shifted flights and for earlier GPS tracks. The axes express eastings and northings in metres, which preserves the geometry of each route rather than reducing the flight to a single number. Each vector is drawn from the same bird's own earlier track.
Vector angle reveals the direction in which a route is displaced, and vector length reveals the size of the displacement. Together the two values describe the offset of a flight from its own history.
11: A **parallel offset** occurs when a flight keeps the shape of a previous route while running consistently to one side of it. The bird keeps its route instead of switching to a straight compass-directed flight. Biro and colleagues measured these offsets with route-relative vectors after the clock shift.

After clock shift, some highly familiar pigeons followed paths displaced to the anticlockwise side of their former tracks. The route-relative vectors kept this lateral bias, with distances expressed in metres and reference rings at 100, 300 and 500 m. The offsets were consistent across the birds that showed them.

A parallel offset shows that landmark attraction and compass influence act together during the same journey. The bird keeps the sequence of turns that its route requires, while the compass shifts the whole route sideways.
12: Group averages can hide distinct individual responses to conflicting cues. In Biro and colleagues' experiment, each highly familiar pigeon's final training flights were paired with its single clock-shifted test flight. Comparing each bird with itself allows retention and disruption of route shape to be seen side by side.

Some shifted pigeons deviated prominently from the learned corridor, some followed parallel offsets, and others reproduced their earlier route closely. The published tracks were rotated to a common reference direction, so the three response types can be read on the same map.
Three different responses to the same clock shift appear among individual birds from one site. Each bird's response depends on how strongly its route is learned.
13: An **initial departure bearing** records the first portion of a homing journey. Landmark and compass influences can change after a bird has already entered a familiar corridor. A bird that leaves in the correct direction can still deviate later, and a bird that leaves poorly can recover.

At Weston Wood, some highly familiar pigeons initially reproduced their route after clock shift and deviated later. Complete GPS trajectories retained this delayed effect. A bearing taken only as the bird left the release site would have recorded the early part of the flight and missed the later deviation.
The timing of a deviation is therefore part of the measured response. A bird's heading can shift several minutes into the flight, and the complete track is what records the moment of the shift.
14: **Multimodal navigation** uses information from more than one sensory system. On familiar pigeon routes, visual landmarks constrain movement while a time-dependent compass continues to influence heading. A recognized landscape keeps the bird close to its route even when the compass signal conflicts with it.

Biro and colleagues' 4 h clock shift produced individual displacement vectors ranging from little route change to pronounced lateral offsets. Many highly familiar birds stayed close to their previous tracks despite the shift. The spread of vectors across birds is the main result of the figure.
Individual birds respond to the same clock shift with very different route changes. The size of each change depends on how familiar the bird is with the landmarks along its route.
15: An **olfactory map** uses learned environmental odor information to estimate position relative to home. An **olfactory activation hypothesis** proposes that smelling unfamiliar odors enables navigation based on other cues, even when the odors carry no location information. The two accounts make different predictions about which odors matter.

Gagliardo and colleagues transported pigeons in containers supplied with natural air, charcoal-filtered air or filtered air plus artificial plant odors. Artificial odor puffs were supplied about every 20 min during transport and while the birds waited at the release site. Each group carried a different odor history into the release.

The activation account predicts that artificial odors should help as much as natural air. The map account predicts that only natural air helps, because only natural air carries the geographical odor signature. The later tracks decide between these predictions.
16: **Anosmia** is loss of the ability to smell. Gagliardo and colleagues anesthetized the olfactory mucosa, the nasal tissue that detects odors, with Xylocaine immediately before release. The same treatment was applied to all three air-exposure groups, so the groups differ only in their earlier odor history.

Birds had already experienced natural air, filtered air or artificial odors during transport and before takeoff. Release occurred at sites 53 km and 61 km from home. The shared nasal treatment reduced new odor sampling during early flight, so the groups' odor histories are compared in isolation.
New odor sampling was limited during early flight in every group. The anesthetic wears off during the journey, so the later part of each track reflects the return of smell.
17: A useful odor treatment must improve navigation, not merely induce movement. Gagliardo and colleagues recorded GPS tracks at 1 Hz after releasing pigeons exposed to different air conditions. The same temporary nasal anesthesia was applied across groups, so the tracks can be compared directly.

Control birds exposed to intact environmental odors showed better homeward movement during the first hour. Filtered-air and artificial-odor birds navigated more poorly at the start of the flight. Artificial odors provided repeated olfactory stimulation, yet they did not restore the homeward performance of the controls.
Natural environmental odors therefore carry information that the bird uses for early homing. The odor mixture of a place sets the direction a bird takes at departure.
18: **Artificial odors** can stimulate olfactory receptors without reproducing the natural relationship between odor mixtures and geographical position. In Gagliardo and colleagues' experiment, plant odors were delivered in filtered air during transport and during the pre-release waiting period. Stimulation was therefore present, but the spatial pattern was absent.

The artificial-odor group matched the controls exposed to environmental air at neither the 53 km nor the 61 km release site. Its GPS tracks often remained tortuous or near the release point, rather than progressing reliably toward home. The artificial-odor birds made less progress toward home than the controls.
Stimulating the nose alone leaves the homing route unorganized. A bird needs odors that vary with position, and artificial plant odors lacked that variation in this experiment.
19: **Tortuosity** describes how winding a path is relative to its net displacement. A pigeon can remain actively flying while making little progress toward home. Total movement and homeward progress are two measures, and the odor results are reported for both.

Gagliardo and colleagues analyzed first-hour flight after releases 53 km and 61 km from the loft. Artificial-odor birds had more tortuous paths and reduced homeward progress than controls. The filtered-air group fell between the two, with paths that were less tortuous than the artificial-odor group's paths.

Winding paths with little progress indicate a failure to orient, while straight paths toward home indicate successful orientation. The measure tells these two outcomes apart for each individual track.
20: The **distance remaining** to the loft measures progress toward the goal, independent of the total path length. A wandering bird may accumulate a long flight without reducing this distance, whereas a directed flight reduces it steadily. Gagliardo and colleagues used this measure alongside the tortuosity values.

One hour after the 53 km release, median distances from home were 29.9 km for controls, 43.8 km for filtered-air birds and 53.5 km for artificial-odor birds. Every group received the same immediate pre-release nasal anesthesia, so the three values reflect differences in odor history.

The control birds had covered the largest share of the distance to home by the end of the first hour. The artificial-odor birds had covered the least, and their median distance remained close to the starting distance.
21: A manipulation can decay during a journey, so time is a variable in the result. Gagliardo and colleagues distinguished the first, second and third hours of GPS tracking. Nasal anesthesia was not assumed to remain equally effective throughout the flight.

Some filtered-air pigeons improved their homeward orientation after the earliest period, consistent with access to natural odors after recovery. Artificial-odor pigeons remained impaired in broader portions of their tracks. The published paths show the same pattern across the three hours.
Recovery of orientation over time shows that the odor deficit is not fixed at departure. Birds can regain the ability to navigate homeward as the nasal block wears off.
22: A **vanishing bearing** is the direction recorded when a released bird disappears from direct observation. It measures the early departure, whereas a complete GPS track includes later circling, stopping, course correction and progress toward home. Gagliardo and colleagues compared bearings with complete tracks for the same birds.

Bearings inferred from early track sections did not fully capture the deficits evident over the first hour and beyond. At the 53 km release, artificial-odor birds could depart in a set direction and then make little homeward progress. The full track showed a deficit that the departure alone did not show.
A bird can leave in a reasonable direction and then fail to make progress. The full track is needed to see that failure.
23: **Path integration** estimates displacement from information gathered during movement, and it differs from a learned environmental map. Jorge and colleagues studied young pigeons 7–8 weeks old during displacement or simulated displacement. Gagliardo and colleagues instead assessed complete homing tracks after odor treatments.

Jorge and colleagues compared natural odors, artificial odors and filtered air, including birds exposed at the home loft rather than during transport. They measured activity-related gene expression in the forebrain after each treatment. The sampled subdivisions of the pigeon hippocampal formation were defined from the same sections.
The two studies use different behavioral preparations, and each produces its own pattern of forebrain activity. Displacement and homing flight each produce a distinct pattern of forebrain activity.
24: **c-Fos** is an activity-related gene product whose expression marks recent neuronal activation. **Immunoreactive nuclei** are cells detected by antibody labeling. Their density provides a regional index of activity accumulated over time, rather than an instantaneous record of action potentials.

Jorge and colleagues collected pigeon brains 1–2 h after the odor manipulation and counted c-Fos-labeled nuclei per square millimetre. The sampled regions included the hippocampal formation, olfactory bulb and piriform cortex. Each region gives its own count for each treatment group.

A regional density reflects the activity of many cells at once. The counts show where activity accumulated across the sampled tissue, which is a different measure from the firing of any single neuron.
25: The **dorsolateral hippocampal area** is one subdivision of the pigeon hippocampal formation, distinct from its dorsomedial and triangular subdivisions. Jorge and colleagues measured c-Fos labeling separately in these regions. The separate measurements show where the forebrain response is strongest.

Natural odors during displacement and unfamiliar artificial odors increased dorsolateral activation relative to filtered air. Artificial odor exposure at the home loft also produced activation comparable to the displacement groups. The dorsolateral subdivision responded most strongly to the odor treatments.
Non-home odors reach the dorsolateral hippocampus even when the bird has not been moved. The same region responds to the odor without any displacement.
26: The **dorsal thalamic nucleus** is a brain region that receives inputs relevant to sensory integration. Jorge and colleagues compared this region with subdivisions of the hippocampal formation, using displacement and simulated displacement to separate movement history from odor treatment. Each region has its own pattern across the two conditions.

Dorsal thalamic c-Fos labeling increased in birds that experienced displacement and homing flight. The hippocampal subdivisions did not all follow the same pattern. The dorsolateral response was particularly strong, while the triangular subdivision responded differently.
Displacement and homing flight engage the thalamus and the hippocampus in different proportions. The same flight therefore produces a different regional profile in each structure.
27: **Lateralization** is a difference in function or activity between the left and right sides of the brain. Jorge and colleagues counted c-Fos-labeled nuclei separately in each hemisphere after odor exposure and homing. The counts were kept apart rather than pooled across both sides.

Olfactory treatments affected the hemispheric pattern in the olfactory bulb, the piriform cortex and the hippocampal subdivisions. Dorsolateral and dorsomedial hippocampal responses were consistent with a larger contribution from left-sided tissue to these odor responses.
Left-sided hippocampal tissue responds more strongly to the odor treatments in this experiment. The difference between sides is one of the measured features of the response.
28: The **trigeminal nerve** carries sensory information from the head. Its ophthalmic branch, designated V1, projects to brainstem trigeminal nuclei. Lefeldt and colleagues asked whether changing magnetic fields activate these receiving regions in pigeons.

Birds experienced a constantly changing magnetic field, a compensated zero field, or the changing field after bilateral V1 section. Exposure lasted 3 h. **ZENK**, an activity-related gene product, was detected in the principal and spinal trigeminal nuclei after each exposure, and the pattern across the three groups shows where the changing field acts.

Labeling was highest when the field changed and V1 was intact, and it fell when the field was removed or the nerve was cut. The result links the magnetic stimulus to the peripheral sensory pathway that runs through V1.
29: The **principal sensory nucleus** of the trigeminal nerve, abbreviated PrV, receives ascending sensory input from the head. Its ventral region, PrVv, can be distinguished from the dorsal region using the brainstem anatomy preserved in the source sections. The subdivisions are identified from the same sections.

After 3 h of changing magnetic fields, Lefeldt and colleagues found ZENK labeling concentrated in a crescent-shaped ventral region. Zero-field exposure and bilateral V1 section reduced the response. The micrographs retain a 100 µm scale bar, so the size of the labeled region can be read directly.
The activated region sits in a fixed position within the nucleus, and it is the same region in each bird. Its shape gives the location of the magnetic response within the brainstem.
30: The **spinal trigeminal nucleus**, or SpV, receives descending trigeminal sensory input. Lefeldt and colleagues distinguished medial and lateral subdivisions. The magnetic response is localized to these subdivisions rather than spread across one undifferentiated brainstem region.

The medial subdivision showed the strongest increase under changing magnetic fields, and bilateral V1 section reduced activation. The source sections compare the changing-field, zero-field and sectioned conditions directly, with each subdivision measured in each animal.
The medial SpV response depends on intact V1 afferents, which carry the signal from the head. The response is therefore carried by a defined sensory pathway into the brainstem.
31: **Neuronal tracing** labels the anatomical pathways that leave an injection site. Lefeldt and colleagues introduced cholera toxin B into V1 to identify its central projections. They then compared the labeled afferents with the regions containing ZENK-positive neurons after magnetic stimulation.

V1 fibers terminated in the principal and spinal trigeminal nuclei. The published overlays preserve the spatial relationship between the traced fibers and the activated cells, with 100 µm and 200 µm scales. **Acetylcholinesterase** staining marked the nuclear boundaries, so each subdivision can be located precisely.
The overlap places the magnetic response along a known route from the nerve to the brainstem. The stain keeps the labeled tissue tied to the known anatomy of each nucleus.
32: A **loss-of-function test** interrupts a candidate pathway and measures the remaining response. Lefeldt and colleagues cut both V1 branches and then exposed the birds to the same changing magnetic stimulus used for intact animals. The response was then measured in each group.

Trigeminal activation decreased after section. The **optic tectum**, a midbrain sensory region included as a comparison, did not change appreciably among the magnetic conditions. Counts were collected after 3 h of exposure, and the field and nerve manipulations were compared under the same timing.
The loss of the trigeminal response after section places the trigeminal input on the response pathway. The unchanged optic tectum shows that the effect is specific to the trigeminal system.
33: V1 also carries ordinary mechanical information from the head, so pecking, grooming and contact with the cage could activate its receiving nuclei. Lefeldt and colleagues therefore monitored the pigeons with infrared cameras during the 3 h exposure. The cameras recorded movement and beak contacts throughout the exposure.

Movement and beak contacts were quantified for each bird. Behavior did not explain the regional ZENK increase, which followed the magnetic condition instead. The analysis compared the behavioral counts across the changing, zero-field and sectioned groups.
The magnetic effect on trigeminal labeling is separate from the animals' ordinary movements. Behavior and field exposure therefore produce distinct patterns of labeling.
34: **Magnetite** is an iron oxide that has been proposed as a material for magnetic sensory transduction. Finding iron in tissue identifies the material but not the receptor, because iron also occurs in metabolic storage and immune cells. Treiber and colleagues examined the pigeon beak to determine which cells contain iron.

Treiber and colleagues stained pigeon upper beaks with Prussian blue, which detects ferric iron, and mapped the labeled cells through serial sections. Iron-rich cells occurred in the respiratory epithelium, the subepidermal tissue and the feather follicles. The source preserves the anatomy of each tissue at the same scale.
The stained positions give a map of where iron occurs in the beak. Identifying a receptor requires additional markers of cell type and ultrastructure.
35: A reproducible sensory organ should have an anatomical organization that matches its proposed function. Earlier descriptions assigned magnetoreception to six bilateral iron-rich clusters in the upper beak. That arrangement had to be tested by systematic examination across individual birds.

Treiber and colleagues counted Prussian-blue-positive cells in successive 500 µm increments along the beak. The locations and numbers of these cells varied widely among pigeons, with cells distributed through multiple tissues rather than gathered into six clusters. The variation was measured in every bird.
Iron-positive cells in the beak are arranged differently from the six-cluster description. The cells form a scattered population across several tissues in each bird.
36: **Ultrastructure** is cellular organization resolved with electron microscopy. Treiber and colleagues examined the iron-rich beak cells in three tissue compartments, rather than assuming that their blue staining indicated sensory dendrites. The electron micrographs identify the internal structures of each labeled cell.

The cells contained ferritin-like granules 6–9 nm in diameter, haemosiderin, an aggregated iron-storage material, and membrane-bound iron-containing compartments termed siderosomes. The source micrographs retain 1 µm scale bars and mark the labeled cellular structures.
The internal structures are those of iron storage, which fixes the identity of the labeled cells as storage cells. The granules, haemosiderin and siderosomes are compartments of iron deposition.
37: **Macrophages** are immune cells that engulf material and take part in tissue defense. **MHC II** is a cell-surface antigen-presentation marker expressed by several immune cell types. Treiber and colleagues combined this marker with iron staining to identify the beak cells.

MHC II labeling colocalized with the iron-positive cells in the respiratory epithelium, the subepidermal tissue and the feather follicles. Combined with the ultrastructure and the absence of convincing neuronal-marker labeling, this result identifies the cells as macrophages.
Macrophages in these tissues carry iron as a storage product. The identity of the iron-laden cells rests on several markers taken together.
38: A peripheral cell candidate and a responsive neural pathway are different claims. Treiber and colleagues rejected the identification of the sampled iron-rich beak cells as magnetosensitive neurons, using histology, immune labeling and electron microscopy. Those three methods point to the same conclusion.

Lefeldt and colleagues later found magnetic-field-related ZENK induction in trigeminal nuclei that depended on intact V1 after 3 h of exposure. The induction establishes a pathway-associated response, while the transducer itself remains to be located. The magnetic response therefore runs through V1 without identifying the receptor.

The trigeminal pathway and the beak cells are separate lines of evidence. The beak cells are one line of evidence, and the trigeminal response is a second line that points to a sensory route carrying the signal.
39: A **local field potential**, or LFP, is an extracellular voltage that reflects coordinated activity and transmembrane currents in the surrounding neural tissue. It differs from the isolated action potentials of an identified single neuron. The LFP sums the activity of many cells near the electrode.

Yang and colleagues recorded hippocampal LFPs together with position during outdoor pigeon homing. Electrodes sampled the left hippocampal formation, while the positional recorder tracked the flight. Release sites were more than 0.8 km from the loft, and trials were run under clear weather with low wind.

Simultaneous recording of the population signal and the position makes it possible to link a neural state to a stage of the journey. The shared time base lets each stage be matched to a moment in the recording.
40: **Flight** produces muscle activity and electrode movement that can contaminate neural recordings. **Denoising** estimates signal components and removes the contributions from movement. The processed traces are shown next to the original voltages. Yang and colleagues applied multivariate empirical mode decomposition followed by independent component analysis.

The source preserves raw and processed multichannel hippocampal traces and their time–frequency power. The recordings spanned the transition from initial circling to sustained homeward flight. Both the raw and the cleaned traces are kept in the figure.
The cleaned traces show the same stage-related pattern as the raw traces. The denoised signal therefore keeps the neural activity that the analysis uses.
41: The **initial decision-making stage**, abbreviated DM, is the early circling or exploratory portion of a homing flight. The **en route stage**, abbreviated ER, begins when the bird adopts a more stable direction toward home. These stages are behavioral classifications of the flight rather than measurements of decisions.

Yang and colleagues identified the transition from heading instability and distance to the loft, then aligned hippocampal frequency power to that transition. The published example tracks both flight direction and distance, with the hippocampal power plotted on the same time axis.
The transition point is defined from the flight itself, so the neural data are aligned to behavior. Each recording is then split into the two stages at the same behavioral marker.
42: **Spectral power** measures the contribution of a frequency range to a recorded voltage signal. Yang and colleagues defined theta as 4–12 Hz, beta as 12–30 Hz, low gamma as 30–60 Hz and high gamma as 60–120 Hz. Each band gives its own power value for each stage.

Theta and beta power ratios were higher during initial decision-making than during en route flight. The high-gamma ratio was greater en route, whereas low gamma showed no consistent difference between the stages. The comparisons used paired behavioral stages from the same homing flights.
Each frequency band follows its own pattern across the two stages. The band-specific pattern shows that the stage difference depends on which frequency is measured.
43: **Phase–amplitude coupling** means that the amplitude of a faster oscillation varies with the phase of a slower oscillation. Phase specifies position within a repeated voltage cycle, while amplitude measures the size of the faster component. The coupling is calculated for each pair of frequencies.

Yang and colleagues found stronger coupling between theta phase at 5–8 Hz and beta amplitude at 20–30 Hz during en route navigation than during initial decision-making. The source compares the two stages using the same frequency-by-frequency analysis, applied to the same recordings.
Theta phase organizes the beta amplitude more strongly once the bird is on its way home. The coupling therefore changes with the stage of the flight.
44: A single release location can confound behavioral stage with a particular heading or a piece of terrain. Yang and colleagues alternated among three release sites more than 0.8 km from the loft. Initial and en route activity were measured within each direction of approach.

Theta and beta power ratios declined during the transition to en route flight, while high-gamma ratios increased across the sites. Theta–beta coupling also strengthened en route. The route maps and paired measurements show these changes at each release site.

The stage effect appears at all three release sites, so the change follows the transition itself rather than one heading. The same change in neural activity accompanies the transition to homeward flight from each direction.
45: **Experience-dependent plasticity** is a change associated with prior experience. A correlation with repeated journeys points to a change in the circuit without naming the cellular mechanism. Yang and colleagues compared five homing releases while continuing to record hippocampal activity and position.

Routes became more efficient with repeated release experience. The differences between initial and en route theta, beta and high-gamma power narrowed, and the stage difference in theta–beta coupling approached zero. The source figure shows these changes across the five releases.
Repeated flights change the neural stage contrast as well as the route. Each release adds to the experience that narrows the difference between the two stages.
